latest.title: 9 reference guides for anyone working with AWS Security
latest.description:
Over the past few days I started putting together a series of technical guides on AWS security covering everything from detection to attack, response, governance and threat modeling.

The goal was never to create content "copied from the documentation".

I wanted something closer to reality:
what actually happens in cloud environments, how attacks work, how to detect them, how to automate response and most importantly understand the why behind things.

So I organized the beginning into 9 guides:

latest.title: Hello, S3 Files!
latest.description: Amazon S3 Files lets AI systems access S3 like a normal filesystem while using EFS as a smart cache underneath. This removes the need to constantly move data between S3 and EFS, reducing complexity, duplication, and startup delays. It is especially useful for agentic AI systems, where multiple agents need fast shared access to files and memory. In short, S3 Files combines the scalability of S3 with the usability of a filesystem for modern AI workloads.

latest.title: Building AI Agents with Strands SDK, Amazon Nova Pro, and MCP
latest.description: In this blog, I share my hands-on learning experience from the Builders Skill Sprint challenge organized by AWS User Group Madurai. Starting from local AI agents with Ollama to building MCP-powered AI assistants using Amazon Bedrock and Strands SDK, this journey helped me understand tool calling, persistent memory, streaming responses, and modern Agentic AI workflows through practical implementation.

latest.title: AWS EFS vs S3 for ML & Agentic Systems
latest.description: The article explains how Amazon EFS and S3 serve different roles in modern ML and agentic AI systems. EFS acts like a shared filesystem ideal for training, fine-tuning, and multi-agent collaboration, while S3 provides scalable and cheap long-term object storage. Most architectures combine both, using S3 as a data lake and EFS as a fast staging layer. However, this creates inefficiencies like data duplication, slower startup times, and extra operational complexity.

trending.title: AIdeas Finalist: ASET – Academic Safety and Evidencing Truth
trending.description:
ASET (Academic Safety and Evidencing Truth) is a scientific claim verification engine built  for the AI era — where information can be generated instantly, but trust cannot, to address the growing problem of hallucinated citations and  AI-generated information.

Instead of probabilistic prediction, ASET retrieves, analyzes, and synthesizes evidence from 1.2M+ indexed research papers to produce literature-backed verification reports for claims extracted from text, documents, webpages, images, and videos.
